questions.q: Why does a stored password hash include the algorithm and its cost parameters, as in $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$salt$hash?
questions.explain: Verification reads the parameters from the stored value, so old and new hashes live side by side. Comparing them with the current parameters tells you which ones to rehash at the next log-in.
options: So the attacker knows how to crack it
So the hash can still be verified after you change the defaults, and so you can detect outdated hashes and upgrade them
Because Argon2id refuses to run without it
To make the hash longer and therefore stronger

questions.q: When can a server upgrade a user's old password hash to Argon2id with new costs?
questions.explain: A hash cannot be turned back into the password, so the new hash must be computed from the password itself. A successful log-in is the natural moment; accounts that never log in again can be forced to reset later.
options: At any time, by re-hashing the stored hash
Only by forcing every user to reset their password
Right after a successful log-in, because only then does the server hold the plain password
When the user logs out

questions.q: Why cap passwords at, say, 1,024 bytes before hashing?
questions.explain: A cap far above any real passphrase costs honest users nothing and bounds the work one request can cause. Check it in bytes, before hashing.
options: Longer passwords are weaker
A slow hash over a huge input is a cheap way for an attacker to burn your CPU: a denial-of-service attack
Argon2id only reads the first 1,024 bytes
Browsers cannot send more than 1,024 bytes in a form

questions.q: What does Argon2id's memory cost (for example 19 MiB per hash) defend against?
questions.explain: Memory-hardness makes each guess need real memory, which is what attackers' hardware lacks. The same memory is a capacity limit on your servers, so plan concurrent log-ins accordingly.
options: Timing attacks on the comparison
Cheap mass guessing on graphics cards and special hardware, which have lots of compute but little memory per core
SQL injection in the users table
Users choosing short passwords

questions.q: Which password policy follows current NIST guidance?
questions.explain: Composition rules and forced changes push people to predictable patterns. Length and refusing known-breached passwords do far more for security.
options: At least 8 characters, one symbol, one digit, and a forced change every 90 days
A minimum length, long passwords allowed, no composition rules, no forced periodic changes, and refusing passwords from breach lists
Exactly 12 characters, letters only
Any password, as long as it is hashed

questions.q: Why does the sessions table store SHA-256 of the session token instead of the token?
questions.explain: Whoever has a live token is logged in. Storing only the hash means a database leak does not leak live sessions.
options: To make sessions expire faster
If the table leaks, the attacker gets hashes that cannot be used as cookies
Because tokens are too long for a text column
To slow down log-in

questions.q: Passwords need a slow hash, but session tokens are hashed with fast SHA-256. Why is that fine?
questions.explain: Slow hashing protects low-entropy secrets that humans choose. A long random token has so much entropy that even billions of guesses per second get nowhere.
options: Session tokens are less important than passwords
The token is 32 random bytes; nobody can guess 2<sup>256</sup> possibilities, so there is nothing to slow down
SHA-256 is slower than Argon2id
Session tokens are never stored

questions.q: A session has a 30-minute idle timeout but no absolute timeout. What is the risk?
questions.explain: The idle clock moves forward on every use. An absolute limit that never moves ends every session eventually, however active.
options: Users are logged out too often
A session (including a stolen one) that is used at least every 30 minutes never expires
The session table grows too slowly
None; idle timeouts are enough

questions.q: What is session fixation, and what prevents it?
questions.explain: If log-in upgrades the existing session in place, whoever knew its token before is now logged in too. A fresh token on every privilege change breaks that link.
options: A session that never expires; prevented by an idle timeout
An attacker plants a known session token in the victim's browser and it becomes logged in when the victim logs in; prevented by issuing a new token at log-in
Two users sharing a session; prevented by HTTPS
A session cookie that is too long; prevented by base64url

questions.q: Which statement about an HS256 JWT is true?
questions.explain: The header and payload are only base64url-encoded. Never put secrets or private data in a JWT.
options: Its payload is encrypted with the secret
Anyone holding it can read the payload; the signature only stops them from changing it
It cannot be decoded without the secret
It is safe to put the user's password in it

questions.q: A verifier reads alg from the token's header and uses that algorithm to check the signature. What is the attack?
questions.explain: The token must not choose how it is verified. The server fixes the allowed algorithm(s) and rejects everything else.
options: The attacker sends a very long token
The attacker sets alg to none (or another algorithm the verifier mishandles), changes the payload and drops the signature
The attacker reuses an expired token
The attacker changes the typ field

questions.q: What is the kid header for, and what must the verifier check about it?
questions.explain: During rotation, new tokens use the new key while old ones are still accepted. An attacker-supplied kid must never reach a file path, a database query or an object's prototype.
options: It is the user id; check that the user exists
It names the key that signed the token, enabling key rotation; the verifier must only accept ids of its own configured keys
It is a random nonce; check that it is unique
It is the token's expiry; check that it is in the future

questions.q: Two services share a signing key. Why must each check the aud (audience) claim?
questions.explain: The audience says who the token is for. Without the check, a token leaked from the less protected service works everywhere the key is shared.
options: To know which language to answer in
Otherwise a token issued for one service is accepted by the other
Because aud contains the expiry time
It is optional and only for logging

questions.q: Why do JWT verifiers allow a small leeway (for example 30 seconds) on exp and nbf?
questions.explain: Clock skew between machines is normal. A small leeway avoids spurious failures without meaningfully extending a token's life.
options: To let users keep expired tokens for longer
Servers' clocks differ slightly; without leeway, a fresh token can be rejected by a server whose clock runs a little ahead
Because JWT times are in minutes
To make brute force harder

questions.q: A web shop's browser app talks only to its own backend. A user reports their laptop stolen. Which design lets you cut the thief off immediately with the least extra machinery?
questions.explain: Revocation is a row deletion with sessions. A stateless JWT stays valid until it expires unless you add a denylist, which brings back the lookup that JWTs were meant to avoid.
options: Stateless JWTs with a 24-hour expiry
Server-side sessions: delete the user's session rows
Tokens stored in localStorage
Basic authentication on every request

questions.q: With refresh-token rotation, an already-used refresh token is presented again. What should the server do?
questions.explain: A used token coming back means two parties hold copies, and the server cannot tell which is the thief. Revoking the family is the only safe answer; the real user just logs in again.
options: Accept it once more, in case of a network retry
Ignore it and keep the family active
Treat it as theft: revoke every token in that family, so both the thief and the user must log in again
Issue a longer-lived token

questions.q: Why is an HttpOnly cookie a better home for a session token than localStorage?
questions.explain: XSS still lets an attacker act within the page while it is open, but it cannot copy an HttpOnly session token away for later use.
options: Cookies are encrypted by the browser
Any JavaScript on the page can read localStorage, so one XSS bug leaks every token; page JavaScript cannot read an HttpOnly cookie
localStorage is cleared on every page load
Cookies are never sent to the server

questions.q: What does naming a cookie __Host-session guarantee?
questions.explain: The prefix closes the route where a compromised or careless subdomain plants a session cookie for the main site, one way to carry out session fixation.
options: The cookie is encrypted
Browsers only accept it with Secure, Path=/ and no Domain, so subdomains cannot set or overwrite it
The cookie expires when the host restarts
The cookie is only sent to localhost

questions.q: What is the problem with "lock the account for one hour after 5 wrong passwords"?
questions.explain: A hard lock turns your defence into a denial-of-service tool. Progressive delays, per-IP limits and second factors slow guessers without letting them lock out customers.
options: It is too gentle on attackers
Anyone who knows a user's e-mail can lock them out on purpose, again and again
It needs a second database
It reveals the password's length

questions.q: Credential stuffing tries one leaked password per account across 50,000 accounts. Which defence does the most against it?
questions.explain: Each account sees only one attempt, so per-account counting never triggers. Limits per source slow the attack, and a second factor makes a correct leaked password insufficient.
options: Per-account progressive delays
Per-IP rate limits plus a second factor (and refusing known-breached passwords)
A longer session timeout
Hashing passwords with SHA-256 twice

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: No key is needed to read a JWT. That is why tokens carry ids and roles, never secrets.
options: { sub: '7', role: 'customer' }
Error: the payload is encrypted
signature

questions.q: A verifier checks expiry with a 30-second leeway. What does this print?
questions.explain: A token that expired 10 seconds ago is within the leeway; 31 seconds ago is not. A token without exp is treated as expired: a verifier must require it, or tokens that never expire slip through.
options: [ false, false, true, true ]
[ false, true, true, false ]
[ false, false, true, false ]
[ false, true, true, true ]

questions.q: A session was created at minute 0 with a 30-minute idle timeout and a 12-hour absolute timeout. It is used at the times listed. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each use moves the idle clock: 20, 45 and 74 are each less than 30 minutes after the previous use. At 110 the session has been idle for 36 minutes, so it is gone.
options: [ true, true, true, false ]
[ true, false ]
[ true, true, true, true ]
[ true, true, false ]

questions.q: What delays does this progressive throttle produce, in seconds?
questions.explain: Five attempts are free, then the delay doubles from one second, capped at 15 minutes (900 s). 214 would be over four hours, which the cap prevents.

questions.explain: in also looks at the prototype chain, where constructor and __proto__ live. An attacker-chosen kid would then pick a function or an object as the "key". Object.hasOwn accepts only your own keys.

2026-08 false false

questions.q: A refresh token store with reuse detection. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first refresh rotates to rt-2. Presenting rt-1 again is reuse, so the whole family, including rt-2, is deleted. The honest client's next refresh finds nothing and must log in again.
options: rt-2 reuse: family revoked unknown
rt-2 rt-3 rt-4
rt-2 reuse: family revoked rt-3
rt-2 unknown unknown

questions.q: Using Web Crypto (available in browsers and Node.js), write async function signJwt(payload, secret) that returns an HS256 JWT: base64url header {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, base64url payload, and the base64url HMAC-SHA256 of header.payload. Print the token for { sub: "7", exp: 1790245000 } with the secret "academy-demo-secret".
questions.explain: Three base64url parts: the first two are readable JSON, the third is the HMAC. The same input and secret always give the same signature, which is what lets a verifier recompute and compare it.

questions.q: Write checkClaims(header, claims, { now, issuer, audience, leeway }) that returns the first problem as a string, in this order: "bad alg" (alg is not HS256), "expired" (no numeric exp, or now > exp + leeway), "wrong issuer", "wrong audience"; otherwise "ok". Times are in seconds.
questions.explain: The fourth token expired 10 seconds ago and is accepted within the 30-second leeway. In a full verifier these checks run only after the signature has been verified; unsigned claims prove nothing.
questions.expected:
ok
bad alg
expired
ok
wrong audience

questions.q: Write createSessions({ idleMs, absoluteMs }) with start(token, userId, now) and read(token, now). read returns the user id, or null (and deletes the session) when it has been idle for idleMs or older than absoluteMs; a successful read moves the idle clock.
questions.explain: Session a is used often enough to stay under the idle limit, but the absolute limit ends it at 100. Session b sat idle for 31 and was deleted, so even the next read finds nothing.

questions.q: Write logIn(sessions, oldToken, userId, newToken) for a Map of token to session. It must copy cart from the old session (if any), delete the old session, and store { userId, cart } under newToken. Print the map's entries afterwards.
questions.explain: The user keeps their cart, but the anonymous token, which someone else might know, is gone. The same step runs at every privilege change.

questions.q: Write createThrottle() with attempt(account, ok, now). Before checking, if now is before the account's nextAt, return "wait N s" (N = seconds left, rounded up). On failure, count it; after the fifth failure each further failure sets nextAt = now + 2^(failures-6) × 1000. On success, reset and return "ok"; on failure return "wrong".
questions.explain: The sixth failure starts a one-second delay, so even the right password at 500 ms must wait. At 1000 ms another failure doubles the delay to two seconds. At 3000 ms it has passed, the right password works, and the counter resets.
questions.expected: wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong, wait 1 s, wrong, wait 1 s, ok

questions.q: Write parsePhc(stored) for strings like $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$c2FsdA$aGFzaA. Return { algorithm, version, params: { m, t, p }, salt, hash } with numbers for version and the params, or null if the string does not have exactly these five parts. Then write needsRehash(stored, current).
questions.explain: Any difference from the current parameters, in either direction, or any other algorithm, means the hash should be replaced at the next successful log-in. A string that does not parse is treated as outdated, never as a match.
questions.expected:
{
  algorithm: 'argon2id',
  version: 19,
  params: { m: 19456, t: 2, p: 1 },
  salt: 'c2FsdA',
  hash: 'aGFzaA'
}
false
true
true

questions.q: Write async function logIn(users, email, password, check) where check(password, hash) is an async password check. It must call check exactly once whether or not the user exists (using DUMMY_HASH for unknown e-mails), and return the same "Wrong e-mail or password" message for both failures. Count the calls.
questions.explain: Every attempt runs exactly one slow check, so response times do not reveal which e-mails have accounts, and the message is identical for both failures.
questions.expected:
welcome, user 7
Wrong e-mail or password
Wrong e-mail or password
